snip.t: Damage control resuscitation uses early blood products and limits crystalloid, accepting a lower blood pressure until haemorrhage is controlled, except in head injury.
Trauma history – recent head injury, fall, road‑traffic accident: Traumatic brain injury is a leading cause of acute ICP rise.

Keep the alternatives open: a mood disorder with psychotic features (mania or depression), substance-induced psychosis (cannabis, khat, alcohol), and a medical or neurological cause (HIV, epilepsy, head injury, thyroid, delirium).
Biological: Family history of depression; HIV or another chronic illness; head injury; alcohol, khat or cannabis use; steroid treatment; poor sleep; postpartum hormonal change
CT or MRI head if first episode after 40–50, focal neurological signs, head injury, confusion or atypical course.

History: onset and course, fever and headache, head injury, diabetes and insulin, drug and alcohol use, new medicines (sedatives, steroids), vomiting and diarrhoea, urinary symptoms, HIV status, liver, kidney or heart disease, and past psychiatric illness.

qs.q: A patient with a head injury develops polyuria and polydipsia with low urine osmolality and hypernatremia. Which medication is the treatment of choice for central diabetes insipidus?
o: Lithium therapy
Spironolactone therapy
Desmopressin therapy
Tolvaptan therapy
qs.e: Desmopressin (DDAVP) is an analog of ADH and is used to treat central diabetes insipidus by replacing the deficient hormone action. Lithium is a well-known cause of nephrogenic diabetes insipidus rather than a treatment.

qs.q: A patient experiences a brief loss of consciousness and temporary respiratory arrest after a head injury. Which of the following best describes the underlying cause of this clinical syndrome?
o: Disruption of the middle meningeal artery
Direct impact causing a focal brain contusion
A change in momentum of the head and brain
Tearing of bridging veins leading to hemorrhage
qs.e: Concussion is a clinical syndrome of altered consciousness following head injury, typically caused by a change in momentum of the head. This change in momentum is thought to dysregulate the reticular activating system, leading to transient neurological dysfunction.
qs.s: CNS Trauma Neuropathology: Fractures, Concussion & CTE: MCQs

qs.q: A patient presents in a coma after a severe head injury, but initial imaging shows no significant contusions or hematomas. Which type of injury should be strongly suspected?
o: Diffuse axonal injury with no surface hematoma
Chronic subdural hematoma from old trauma
Basal skull fracture with associated meningitis
Acute epidural hematoma with rapid expansion
qs.e: Diffuse axonal injury (DAI) is a key cause of coma after trauma, even in the absence of contusions or hematomas, affecting up to 50% of such patients. It involves widespread axonal damage from mechanical forces, often angular acceleration.

qs.q: A patient who suffered a localized head injury struggles to speak, producing broken, effortful sentences with poor grammar, though they clearly understand questions asked by the clinician. Where is the damaged area typically located?
o: Posterior part of the inferior frontal gyrus
Occipital visual association areas
Posterior part of the superior temporal gyrus
Postcentral gyrus of the parietal lobe
qs.e: Broca's area is located in the posterior part of the inferior frontal gyrus in the dominant hemisphere and controls motor speech production. Wernicke's area is in the superior temporal gyrus and handles comprehension.

qs.q: A 25-year-old woman incurs a head injury from a skiing accident. She is now in stable condition and her vital signs are normal. Serum electrolytes now show Na 134 meq/L, K 7.6 meq/L, Cl 100 meq/L, and CO2 25 meq/L. What is the most likely etiology for these laboratory test findings?
o: Mannitol infusion
Excess intravenous fluids
Severe diarrhea
Acute renal failure
qs.e: ** Stable patient with markedly elevated potassium (7.6) but normal other electrolytes suggests pseudohyperkalemia from hemolysis during blood collection, releasing intracellular potassium.
